AlwaysHex - Visual Studio Extension
Show variable values in decimal and hex together while you debug in Visual Studio.
Visual Studio's debugger shows numbers either in decimal
or
in hex. Which one depends on the
Hexadecimal Display
toggle, so you keep switching back and forth. AlwaysHex shows both:
Without AlwaysHex
With AlwaysHex
int a = 100
100
100 (0x00000064)
int neg = -1
-1
-1 (0xffffffff)
int16_t i = 42
42
42 (0x002a)
char ch = 'a'
97 'a'
97 (0x61) 'a'
POINT pt
{x=1655 y=222}
{x=1655 (0x00000677) y=222 (0x000000de)}
The radix you picked with
Hexadecimal Display
always comes first. With hex display on,
100
is shown as
0x00000064 (100)
.
Where it works
Languages:
C and C++ (native code) and C#. C++/CLI is left exactly as Visual Studio shows it.
Windows:
data tips (hover), Watch, Locals, Autos, struct/class members, array elements,
and the Call Stack window
Visual Studio:
2022 and 2026, 64-bit.
Tested:
Visual Studio 2022 17.14 (Community) and Visual Studio 2026 18.11 (Professional)
with the full release tests; also used with Professional 2022.
Installable but not tested:
the installer also accepts every other 2022 version (17.0 and
later), other 2026 versions and the Enterprise edition. AlwaysHex relies on undocumented
debugger behavior (see
How it works
), so on an untested version values may
show one radix only or an evaluation error.
There is nothing to configure: install it and start debugging.
Copying a value:
Copy Value
in the right-click menu copies both parts, for example
100 (0x00000064)
. To copy only the first part, double-click the value and press Ctrl+C.
Good to know:
C#: visualizer windows (IEnumerable, DataTable, …) show their contents in one radix.
C#, remote debugging (Remote Tools): C# values are shown in one radix only, as without
AlwaysHex.
Installation
Download
AlwaysHex.vsix
from the
Releases
page.
Close Visual Studio and double-click the file. The installer lists the Visual Studio
versions it can install into.
Start Visual Studio and debug as usual.
To turn AlwaysHex off, disable it under
Extensions → Manage Extensions
and restart Visual Studio.
Not active after an update in Visual Studio 2026?
After updating an already installed
AlwaysHex, Visual Studio 2026 sometimes keeps using its old extension cache and starts without
it. Close Visual Studio, open a
Developer Command Prompt for VS 2026
and run
devenv /updateconfiguration
once.
How it works
AlwaysHex consists of two components for the Visual Studio debug engine ("Concord"):
C/C++:
a component just above the built-in C/C++ expression evaluator, so every request
for a value reaches it first. It asks the evaluator twice, once in your radix and once in the
other one (without side effects), merges the two answers,
100
+
0x00000064
→
100 (0x00000064)
, and hands the result to Visual Studio.
C#:
a component just above the C# value formatter. When the formatter produces the text
for an integer, AlwaysHex adds the other radix. Nothing else changes, so all C# debugger
features (visualizers, Object IDs, …) keep working, and property getters never run twice.
The source code in
AlwaysHex/AlwaysHexEvaluator.cs
starts
with a detailed explanation, including the debugger terms it uses and the routing trick;
AlwaysHex/AlwaysHexClrFormatter.cs
is the C# part.
Warning
Undocumented Visual Studio behavior
To pass requests on to the built-in C/C++ evaluator, AlwaysHex relies on how Visual Studio routes
them internally. This routing is not documented by Microsoft. It is tested only with Visual Studio
2022 17.14 and Visual Studio 2026 18.11; other versions may behave differently, and a future
version may need an update of AlwaysHex. If the routing changes, C/C++ values may show one radix
only, look different, or show an evaluation error. AlwaysHex has guards that end a request which
keeps coming back to it with an error instead of looping, but it cannot guarantee that Visual Studio
or another debugger component it passes a request on to always answers.

Hi HN, I'm Cody, I have 847 YouTube playlists, and always hated that YouTube failed to provide basic playlist management tools. Ctrl+F was never convenient and breaks past 200 playlists. So I built & shipped my first Chrome extension. It replaces the Save dialog with a native-feeling searchable one that fetches all your playlists (and whether the current video is saved there) directly from YouTube's InnerTube API. It works robustly across every current save surface (watch page, home feed, search results, Shorts via right-click or Alt+S).
This version is faster and more stable than my original attempt. In 1.0 I read and wrote YouTube's DOM directly. It felt like the efficient approach, but makes for constant UI regressions as YouTube changes, so I can't recommend it. In 2.0 the UI lives outside YouTube's app tree in a closed shadow root, and the data comes from YouTube's internal InnerTube JSON API. The trigger it uses is a small hook wrapping the page's fetch, i.e. when YouTube's client requests the add-to-playlist panel.
Privacy: As private as possible given it's a YouTube extension. The extension only talks to youtube.com, doesn't ship any third-party code, and stores nothing about your playlists, just two display preferences: sort order, and the privacy new playlists are created with. AGPL-3.0.
Install:
https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/efgbkmnooapcpdpgmih...
Source:
https://github.com/codyhxyz/playlist-search-extension
Site:
https://playlist.codyh.xyz/
Bonus:
Technically you can replicate the filter-bar functionality with a dev console script, which I've linked here: (
https://gist.github.com/codyhxyz/00001e74d238ae5911ccfc8f8d4...
). For obvious reasons, I prefer a dedicated extension.
Happy to answer anything about my approach including the InnerTube API or about the shadow-root. Always looking to improve the extension's architecture.

Model               Params   Trained On        Cost    PG19 (bits/byte) ↓
MambaByte-972M       0.97B   75 GB (PG19)      ~$4k    0.883
MegaByte-1B          1.02B   80 GB (PG19)      ~$1.6k  1.000

mini-AGI (frozen)    1.26B   2.8 GB (0 PG19)   ~$56    1.995
The published models were trained on PG19's own training books, 75 to 80 GB of them, and are scored on more books like those. mini-AGI has never been trained on PG19 and has read no Victorian novels, so for it these books are completely out of its domain.
There are more details in the repository. The most important part is a difference between "frozen" and "online" attempts where we allow the model to specialize on the task as it goes through the evaluation dataset. Clearly showcasing the power of continual learning regime simply unavailable for any other typical LLM.

Loböle
Open-source parametric CAD: B-Rep modeling on OpenCASCADE, a Vulkan
viewport, and one command layer that the GUI, Python scripts and AI agents
all drive. Linux first; Windows builds exist, macOS is untested.
Version 0.1: so expect some rough edges. Issues are welcome.
What it does
Parametric modeling:
a constraint sketcher, features that survive
upstream edits (stable topological naming), variables and expressions,
configurations, sheet metal, bent tube.
Assemblies:
mates, sub-assemblies, motion studies with clash checks,
exploded views, a BOM, standard fasteners.
Drawings:
sheets with projected views, dimensions and tables, out to
SVG and PDF.
Simulation:
static and modal FEM, and topology optimization, on the
part itself.
Manufacturing:
2.5D, 3-axis and 4th-axis milling posted for Mach3,
LinuxCNC or GRBL, each file verified by simulating it; checks for 3D
printing.
Versioning:
history, named versions, branches and merges, backed by
git.
Scripting and agents:
JSON-RPC, a Python SDK and an MCP server reach
every command the GUI has; a terminal panel runs an agent inside the
window.
Interchange:
STEP, IGES, STL, OBJ and BREP in, and DXF and SVG into a
sketch; STEP, STL, BREP, glTF, OBJ, PLY, DXF, SVG and PDF out.
Warning
CAM has cut real parts on one machine only
: a 6090 CNC router on
Mach3. Simulate and dry-run every file before cutting.
lobole-demo-1080p.mp4
Gallery
Every model here is built by a generator, an ordinary Python program driving
the API;
generators/README.md
lists them all.
OM615 diesel
(Opus 5.5): every part down to the bearing shells, with its injection pump chained to the crank and timed
Automatic watch
(Opus 5, one shot): a 3 Hz self-winding movement, with lever escapement, rotor winding and keyless works
Bicycle
(Opus 5.5, one shot): modelled from photographs
5-inch FPV quadcopter
(Opus 5, one shot): 91 occurrences, fitted fasteners, FEM on the arms
Installing
From the
releases page
:
Linux:
lobole-<version>-x86_64.AppImage
, the full GUI on glibc
2.39 or newer (Ubuntu 24.04, Debian 13, Fedora 40 and later).
chmod +x
it and run it; linked onto your PATH as
lobole
, the MCP server can
start it by itself.
Ubuntu 26.04:
sudo apt install ./lobole_<version>-1_amd64.deb
.
Windows:
a zip or an installer. Tested on Windows by hand and
under Wine on every release, unsigned (SmartScreen warns), no FEM.
Linux, headless:
an AppImage with the engine and its JSON-RPC
interface, no window, for servers (
caveats
).
Elsewhere:
Nix:
nix run github:eliasaronson/lobole
, the full GUI. Outside
NixOS the GUI needs
nixGL
.
Container:
ghcr.io/eliasaronson/lobole-headless
(
below
).
Python:
pip install lobole
, the client, SDK and MCP server
(
docs/scripting
).
Other distributions:
build from source
.
Requirements
Ubuntu 24.04:
CI installs exactly this list on every push:
sudo apt install git cmake ninja-build build-essential python3 \
libvulkan-dev glslc libglfw3-dev libglm-dev \
libspdlog-dev libgtk-3-dev nlohmann-json3-dev libeigen3-dev libboost-dev \
libocct-data-exchange-dev libocct-modeling-algorithms-dev libocct-modeling-data-dev \
libocct-foundation-dev libocct-ocaf-dev libocct-visualization-dev \
libtbb-dev libvterm-dev
Ubuntu 26.04:
the same list, plus
libnglib-dev netgen python3-netgen libspectra-dev
for FEM meshing and modal analysis; CI installs that too. The last two are needed only because
Ubuntu's Netgen CMake config checks for them.
Nix / NixOS:
nix-shell
in the repo root pins everything. The Vulkan
driver comes from your system (
hardware.graphics.enable = true
).
Flatpak:
tools/flatpak-build.sh
builds for any distribution
(
packaging/flatpak/
).
Other distributions:
the Ubuntu list says what is needed; OpenCASCADE
must be 7.6 or newer, CMake 3.14+, and the compiler C++23.
Windows
cross-compiles from Linux (
packaging/windows/
).
macOS
is
untested.
Clone with
--recurse-submodules
(or run
git submodule update --init --recursive
) for the vendored dependencies.
Optional parts
cmake
prints which optional features it compiled in. CAM and the terminal
panel can be switched off (
-DENABLE_CAM=OFF
,
-DENABLE_TERMINAL=OFF
), and
then they do not exist at all. Without
Netgen
there is no FEM meshing,
and without
Spectra
no modal analysis; Ubuntu has both from 26.04 on,
and every release download except Windows carries them.
On OpenCASCADE 7.6 (Ubuntu 24.04), PLY export is missing and some booleans
come out wrong (
details
).
Building
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja
cmake --build build
cmake --install build --prefix "$HOME/.local"   # optional: app, assets, desktop entry
Without Dear ImGui Test Engine
The test engine is the one dependency that is not open source: a company
over 2M USD turnover that builds or ships Loböle needs a paid licence from
DISCO HELLO.
-DENABLE_TEST_ENGINE=OFF
removes it, along with the GUI test

ui_action
tier.

build/lobole [-f path/to/file.step]

The engine and its JSON-RPC interface, no GPU or display, with the full
feature set (OpenCASCADE 7.9, Netgen, Spectra):
docker run --rm -p 8437:8437 ghcr.io/eliasaronson/lobole-headless
lobole-remote 8437 get_state          # from pip install lobole
nix build .#dockerHeadless
builds the same image.
Caution
The JSON-RPC interface is
unauthenticated and can read and write
files
. The image listens on all interfaces so the published port works;
never publish it on a network you do not trust.
Testing
tools/ctest -LE gui -j$(nproc)    # headless: no GPU, no display
./tools/gui-tests-xvfb.sh         # the GUI suite on a virtual display
More in
CONTRIBUTING.md
.
Remote control
With an AI agent:
install the MCP server and register it, e.g. with
Claude Code. It attaches to a running Loböle, or starts one without a
window if none is running:
uv tool install lobole            # or: pip install lobole
claude mcp add lobole -- lobole-mcp
Scripts drive a live session over JSON-RPC (localhost only, opt-in):
./lobole --remote 8437     # or --headless --remote 8437, with no GPU
export PYTHONPATH=$PWD/python
python3 -m lobole.client 8437 get_state
python3 -m lobole.client 8437 add_feature \
'{"feature": {"type": "Box", "name": "Box 1", "on": "Top",
"width": 2, "depth": 2, "height": 2}}'
Every GUI command is reachable, plus UI actions that click and type in the
real window. See the
Python SDK
and the
MCP server
.

editor's UI chrome — a custom

apply.sh
writes.

Surface
Value
Sidebar, chrome (title/toolbar), panes
#2e3440

Elevated surfaces — menus, dropdowns, meta panels
#3b4252
(nord1)
Base foreground
#d8dee9
(nord4)
Accent / focus ring
#88c0d0

Git status (modified/removed/untracked)
#ebcb8b
/

/
#a3be8c
Terminal ANSI palette
full Nord mapping (see

)

.

python3

)

git clone https://github.com/willio/nord-theme-for-cursor.git
cd
nord-theme-for-cursor
#

fully quit Cursor first

Unofficial community mod; not affiliated with Anysphere/Cursor. The Nord palette is by

takes.

- [author] ppcvote: Hi HN. I run a one-person company in Taiwan. MindThread is a Threads scheduler with paying users here, and it already had a REST API. This release wraps it for agents: a CLI (`npx mindthread-cli`) and an MCP server (`npx -y mindthread-mcp`, or hosted at https://mindthread.tw/api/mcp , registry id io.github.ppcvote/mindthread). Your agent can draft posts in the account's voice, publish or schedule text, images, carousels and video, work a queue, read insights, and review reply drafts from "cloud patrol", which searches Threads for your keywords. Everything in this release goes through Meta's official Threads API, so no passwords. (A separate, Taiwan-only browser extension exists and is not part of this.) The part I care about most is control. Each key has allow, ask or deny per permission (publish now, schedule, send replies, turn on patrol). With ask, the call returns `approval_required` and a link, and nothing goes out until the owner confirms on mindthread.tw. In the CLI that is exit code 3, so the agent stops instead of retrying. Defaults for a new live key: publish now, sending replies, enabling patrol and loosening guardrails ask first; scheduling a post 30+ minutes ahead is allowed, and you can set it to ask. Content rules (length, banned phrases, only numbers from your fact list) are checked by the server on every API write and again at publish time. With `enforce: block` a violating post is refused; the default is `warn`, which only flags it. Limits: Threads only. Free plan is 1 account, 3 posts a day and 50 calls a day per live key, and Meta's per-profile caps apply on top. The MCP server lacks the thread, webhook and A/B tools the CLI has. The CLI and bridge are MIT; the service is hosted. No signup needed to look around: `curl https://mindthread.tw/api/mcp ` lists the tools, and `tools/list`, `get_playbook` and `list_formulas` work without a key. - [author] ppcvote: Hi HN. I run a one-person company in Taiwan. MindThread is a Threads scheduler with paying users here, and it already had a REST API. This release wraps it for agents: a CLI (`npx mindthread-cli`) and an MCP server (`npx -y mindthread-mcp`, or hosted at https://mindthread.tw/api/mcp , registry id io.github.ppcvote/mindthread). Your agent can draft posts in the account's voice, publish or schedule text, images, carousels and video, work a queue, read insights, and review reply drafts from "cloud patrol", which searches Threads for your keywords. Everything in this release goes through Meta's official Threads API, so no passwords. (A separate, Taiwan-only browser extension exists and is not part of this.) The part I care about most is control. Each key has allow, ask or deny per permission (publish now, schedule, send replies, turn on patrol). With ask, the call returns `approval_required` and a link, and nothing goes out until the owner confirms on mindthread.tw. In the CLI that is exit code 3, so the agent stops instead of retrying. Defaults for a new live key: publish now, sending replies, enabling patrol and loosening guardrails ask first; scheduling a post 30+ minutes ahead is allowed, and you can set it to ask. Content rules (length, banned phrases, only numbers from your fact list) are checked by the server on every API write and again at publish time. With `enforce: block` a violating post is refused; the default is `warn`, which only flags it. Limits: Threads only. Free plan is 1 account, 3 posts a day and 50 calls a day per live key, and Meta's per-profile caps apply on top. The MCP server lacks the thread, webhook and A/B tools the CLI has. The CLI and bridge are MIT; the service is hosted. No signup needed to look around: `curl https://mindthread.tw/api/mcp ` lists the tools, and `tools/list`, `get_playbook` and `list_formulas` work without a key. A free account gives you a `mt_test_` sandbox key. A `mt_test_` key simulates every write. Feedback I want: is per-permission ask the right granularity, and what would you need before letting an agent post for you?

- [author] ppcvote: Hi HN. I run a one-person company in Taiwan. MindThread is a Threads scheduler with paying users here, and it already had a REST API. This release wraps it for agents: a CLI (`npx mindthread-cli`) and an MCP server (`npx -y mindthread-mcp`, or hosted at https://mindthread.tw/api/mcp , registry id io.github.ppcvote/mindthread). Your agent can draft posts in the account's voice, publish or schedule text, images, carousels and video, work a queue, read insights, and review reply drafts from "cloud patrol", which searches Threads for your keywords. Everything in this release goes through Meta's official Threads API, so no passwords. (A separate, Taiwan-only browser extension exists and is not part of this.) The part I care about most is control. Each key has allow, ask or deny per permission (publish now, schedule, send replies, turn on patrol). With ask, the call returns `approval_required` and a link, and nothing goes out until the owner confirms on mindthread.tw. In the CLI that is exit code 3, so the agent stops instead of retrying. Defaults for a new live key: publish now, sending replies, enabling patrol and loosening guardrails ask first; scheduling a post 30+ minutes ahead is allowed, and you can set it to ask. Content rules (length, banned phrases, only numbers from your fact list) are checked by the server on every API write and again at publish time. With `enforce: block` a violating post is refused; the default is `warn`, which only flags it. Limits: Threads only. Free plan is 1 account, 3 posts a day and 50 calls a day per live key, and Meta's per-profile caps apply on top. The MCP server lacks the thread, webhook and A/B tools the CLI has. The CLI and bridge are MIT; the service is hosted. No signup needed to look around: `curl https://mindthread.tw/api/mcp ` lists the tools, and `tools/list`, `get_playbook` and `list_formulas` work without a key. A free account gives you a `mt_test_` sandbox key. A `mt_test_` key simulates every write. Feedback I want: is per-permission ask the right granularity, and what would you need before letting an agent post for you?

repeatable evaluations

. This forecast underscores the need to review AI system security, configurations, integrations, and access controls as systems evolve.

sensitive data
reaching an unsuitable provider. In addition, a coding agent may also follow outdated requirements or introduce a defect that a single test run misses.

How GeekyAnts Versions AI Models, Prompts, and Coding Tools
Claude Code is the primary coding assistant described across the recent documented projects. Some engineers have also used Cursor, OpenAI Codex, and opencode alongside or instead of Claude Code. These examples reflect tools used by individual engineers, not a confirmed company-wide approved list.
The models used in product features are a separate decision. Provider choice depends on the task and project. The clinical education platform uses Google Gemini in production and supports other options, including Anthropic Claude, OpenAI, OpenRouter, and self-hosted models through Ollama. uses Anthropic Claude models.

In the clinical education platform, the documented evaluation workflow requires prompt changes to include an updated evaluation baseline in the same commit; this is intended to help reviewers assess how changes affect results. The family-records app pins model versions to dated releases to avoid unexpected changes from moving provider aliases.
The GeekyAnts
internal projects use tagged plugin versions and run records to capture the plugin version, configuration, and starting code revision. These records help engineers trace unexpected results to a specific version or configuration, while
code review
and repeatable evaluations help teams assess AI behavior before proceeding.
GeekyAnts’ Approach in Tracking AI Performance, Errors, and Model Changes
The clinical education platform records each AI call’s provider and model, response time, status, retry attempts, errors, token usage, and content. It also captures the reason a call finished. These records help engineers investigate unexpected model behavior and trace individual requests. If performance signals change, they can compare results against the evaluation baseline and rerun relevant tests before approving a prompt, model, or configuration change.
In
healthcare software
, similar traceability can help teams review how an AI-assisted feature handled clinical information or generated a result, where those records are captured by the system. The platform’s wider observability stack includes monitoring tools, but AI calls do not yet have dedicated Prometheus metrics. Engineers can query the AI audit records to investigate call behavior.
The family-records app tracks model latency, errors, usage, missing fields, and other session-level signals without storing audio. The app automatically deletes transcripts and drafts 24 hours after each session ends. This is especially important in healthcare applications, where teams must decide which information needs to be kept for care-related workflows and which should be deleted to reduce unnecessary exposure of sensitive data.
Tracking AI Runs, Detecting Performance Drift, and Maintaining Audit Trails
The internal GeekyAnts
projects use evaluation reports and run ledgers to track task progress, review outcomes, model behavior, and costs. The records also capture the plugin version, workflow configuration, and starting code revision, which helps engineers trace a run to the setup under which it began.
Across the projects, changes in retries, missing fields, latency, and cost can indicate that a model, prompt, or provider needs review. More retries may indicate a failing request path. Missing fields can suggest an extraction problem, while slower responses or rising costs may follow a model or configuration change. Teams can use these findings to investigate and rerun evaluations.
Audit needs depend on the feature. An AI-generated clinical examination score may require records of the model and output for later review, while storing raw user content can create unnecessary exposure elsewhere. Keeping relevant records helps teams investigate failures and explain how a system produced a result.
How GeekyAnts Manages AI Data Retention, Provider Selection, and Hosting
Before adding an AI feature, teams need to know what data it sends to a provider, what stays in the application, and how long records remain available. Retention requirements depend on the feature and project; one rule does not fit every workflow.
The family-records app does not store audio. It temporarily retains transcripts and drafts, which are deleted by an hourly cleanup job once 24 hours have passed since the session ended. The clinical education platform takes a different approach. It retains AI call content in the client’s database because scoring decisions may need to be reviewed later. The retention approach depends on whether the records are needed to review a decision later.
Evaluating AI Providers, Data Retention, and Fallback Options
Provider selection requires assessing the terms for the specific engagement. These checks should cover processing regions, retention periods, training practices, and subprocessors. Vendor approval processes, contractual commitments, and subprocessor disclosures should be verified for each engagement rather than assumed to be company-wide policies.
If a project supports alternative providers, teams can evaluate a replacement against the relevant quality and security checks before switching. Rollback options depend on the implementation. The internal
ga
project uses tagged plugin releases and version-controlled code, while product features may have task-specific fallbacks, such as a manual form when voice functionality fails. Switching providers or leaving a vendor may also require configuration or integration changes, so the available options need to be assessed for each engagement.
Engineering assistants raise a separate question, as the tool’s technical settings do not guarantee particular contract terms or private deployment arrangements. The available documentation does not establish a universal right for every client to prohibit AI or mandate specific tools. A clear account of data flows, retention, and available provider options gives clients a basis for making informed decisions before starting the implementation process.
What Happens When AI Changes Go Unchecked?
An untested code or configuration change can disrupt workflows, break integrations, or expose sensitive data. Repeatable evaluations, traceable changes, and relevant audit records help teams identify defects and investigate failures before they affect users.

Live translation

Nothing leaves your computer
No account, no cloud, no telemetry. Your audio and text are processed locally and never uploaded.
Hear it back
Play any translation aloud with your system's built-in voice for that language.
Record meetings
Meeting mode transcribes for as long as you talk, saves a timestamped transcript and its translation as it goes, and keeps your computer awake until you stop.

Snaparser turns Snapchat exports into a searchable local archive.
The parser, SQLite database, and HTMX frontend run in one Go binary.

your
data
.
It can be used to view your login history, account info, snap
& chat history metadata and a bunch of other useful stuff.
However, there is no search or filtering.
If you want to use it, run the command below:
$ python3 -m http.server --directory data/
with data holding the content of your unzipped data
If you want a more powerful ui, continue reading...
Installation
Install with go:
$ go install github.com/vanillaiice/snaparser/v2/cmd/snaparser@latest
Or download from
releases
.
Usage
Download and unzip your Snapchat export by following the guide on Snapchat's
website
.
Start the browser without supplying paths:
$ snaparser serve
#
http://127.0.0.1:8080
If there is no existing archive, the browser opens setup with an in-page folder
browser.
Browse to the unzipped Snapchat export and click
Use this folder
, or enter
its path directly. Processing runs in the background, and the archive opens
automatically when it finishes. The folder browser reads folders on the machine
running Snaparser.
The
Archive
button lets you select another export or
Rebuild archive
from the saved export. Both actions refresh the database and attachment index
without restarting the server. A failed operation preserves the previous archive.
The selected path is saved in the database and reused on later launches.
To import immediately from the command line:
$ snaparser serve --data ./data
--data
requires the unchanged export root containing
json/
and
chat_media/
.
Keep this directory in place: the viewer reads attachments from it.
--db

SQLite path (default
snaparser.db
). To import without serving, then reuse the
archive and its recorded media directory:
$ snaparser import --data ./data --db archive.db
$ snaparser serve --db archive.db
Importing replaces the current backup only after all required JSON files parse
successfully and additional JSON files validate. Missing directories, missing
supported files, or invalid JSON
abort the import without changing an existing archive.
The browser includes:
Chats:
full-text search, conversation browsing, older history, links from
search results to surrounding messages, and image/video/audio attachments.
Friends:
searchable relationship lists, including blocked, deleted, pending,
ignored, hidden suggestions, and sent requests. Click a name to open its chat;
friends without an imported conversation are marked “No chat history.”
Snap history:
the same conversation sidebar, incoming/outgoing bubbles,
search, surrounding-record links, and older-history navigation as chats.
Snaps show exported metadata; snap history does not contain attachment IDs.
Calls:
incoming/outgoing filters, literal text search, dates, results,
duration, location, and network information.
Account:
account/device details, login/device histories, public and app
profiles, engagement, content categories, and paged
account changes.

Turn incoming email into webhooks. A small, self-hosted SMTP server that checks each email against your rules and sends the matches to your webhooks, with a web UI to see what arrived and how each webhook responded.

Bank and card alerts
→ your budgeting app (Firefly III, Actual)
Receipts and invoices
→ Paperless-ngx or your accounting tool
Monitoring alerts
→ ntfy, Slack, Discord, PagerDuty
A support address
→ your helpdesk (Zammad, Linear, a custom API)
Shipping notifications
→ Home Assistant
Anything else
→ n8n, Zapier-style automations, your own service

All you need is Docker. This starts mailrelay plus a small echo server that serves as a test webhook:
curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gowthamgts/mailrelay/main/docker-compose.quickstart.yaml

curl

'
EOF
'

To: hello@example.com
Subject: Hello from mailrelay
It works!
EOF

http://localhost:2623
. The email is there, marked
Dropped
because no rule matched yet.

Rules → New rule
, leave the conditions empty (matches everything) and set the webhook URL to
http://echo:8080/
.
Open the email and click
Replay
. It is now
Delivered
, and the response body shows exactly what your webhook received.
Clean up with
docker compose -f docker-compose.quickstart.yaml down -v
.
Deploy
Docker.
For a real server, start from
docker-compose.example.yaml
, or:
docker run -d --name mailrelay \
-p 25:25 -p 127.0.0.1:2623:2623 \
-v mailrelay_data:/data \
-e MAILRELAY_SMTP__DOMAIN=mx.example.com \
ghcr.io/gowthamgts/mailrelay:latest
Add
-e MAILRELAY_WEBHOOK__ALLOW_PRIVATE_NETWORKS=true
if your webhooks point at services on your network. The image keeps everything under
/data

.eml
files, and an optional
config.yaml

Download a release from the
releases page
, or build it with

. Then run

.

The web UI has no login unless you configure
http.auth
(OIDC). Keep port 2623 on localhost, or put it behind a reverse proxy that handles auth. Also set
smtp.allowed_recipients
so only your addresses are accepted.

SMTP ──▶ SPF / DKIM / DMARC ──▶ rule matching ──▶ webhooks (async, with retries)
(off | log | enforce)          every matching rule fires
mailrelay replies
250 OK
as soon as it accepts an email. Webhooks are sent in the background with exponential backoff, so a slow or failing webhook never bounces mail. Every attempt is recorded, and any email can be replayed from the UI.

Rules are created in the web UI and take effect immediately. Each rule has
conditions
and a
webhook
.

to ignore case).
Match all or any
of the conditions. A rule with no conditions matches every email.

mailrelay
Turn incoming email into webhooks. A small, self-hosted SMTP server that checks each email against your rules and sends the matches to your webhooks, with a web UI to see what arrived and how each webhook responded.
Point an MX record (or a forwarding rule) at mailrelay and wire email into the things that only speak HTTP:
Bank and card alerts
→ your budgeting app (Firefly III, Actual)
Receipts and invoices
→ Paperless-ngx or your accounting tool
Monitoring alerts
→ ntfy, Slack, Discord, PagerDuty
A support address
→ your helpdesk (Zammad, Linear, a custom API)
Shipping notifications
→ Home Assistant
Anything else
→ n8n, Zapier-style automations, your own service
Quick start
All you need is Docker. This starts mailrelay plus a small echo server that serves as a test webhook:
